title: Wildfire smoke, indoor and outdoor PM2.5, and sick-related absenteeism in Oklahoma Head Start early care and education centers
abstract: Background Wildfire smoke can infiltrate early care and education (ECE) buildings, yet evidence remains limited for children from birth to age 5, non-Western U.S. regions, and smoke-mitigation strategies in childcare classrooms. Objective We examined wildfire smoke, indoor and outdoor PM 2.5 , and sick-related absenteeism in Oklahoma Head Start Centers. Methods We analyzed Cohort 1 of the OK-AIR cluster-randomized 2×2 factorial trial, including 5 centers, 20 classrooms, and 204 children during 2023-2024. Classrooms were randomized to control, portable HEPA filtration, upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI), or HEPA + UVGI. Indoor PM 2.5 was monitored continuously and paired with hourly EPA outdoor PM 2.5 . Wildfire smoke-impacted and non-impacted days during February-March 2024 were identified using NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke plumes. Indoor-outdoor PM 2.5 relationships during smoke-impacted days were modeled using ordinary least squares regression. This analysis compared pooled Baseline and Intervention periods rather than arm-specific effects. Sick-related absenteeism was modeled across 4 centers and 16 classrooms using a binomial generalized linear model with a 7-day rolling average of the NASA FIRMS/VIIRS regional fire-detection metric. Results Indoor PM 2.5 was higher on smoke-impacted days than on non-impacted days. After adjustment for outdoor PM 2.5 , the intervention-period indicator was associated with 29.0% lower indoor PM 2.5 during smoke-impacted days (95% CI: 22.8-34.7%), and this contrast did not isolate HEPA, UVGI, or their combination. Each 100-detection increase in the 7-day rolling mean of regional fire detections was associated with higher odds of sick-related absence (OR = 1.106, 95% CI: 1.018-1.201, p = 0.018). The wildfire-by-period interaction was imprecise, and the data were insufficient to detect or exclude meaningful effect modification. Significance Wildfire smoke was associated with higher indoor PM 2.5 , and regional wildfire activity was associated with sick-related absenteeism. Lower PM 2.5 during Intervention periods was consistent with a possible contribution from filtration, but the period-based analysis did not estimate an arm-specific HEPA effect. Impact Wildfire smoke is an important exposure concern in ECE settings, but evidence remains limited for birth-to-five classrooms and for regions outside the western U.S. Using classroom-level indoor PM 2.5 monitoring, EPA outdoor measurements, NOAA HMS smoke plumes, FIRMS/VIIRS fire detections, and daily attendance records, we found elevated indoor PM 2.5 on smoke-impacted days and higher odds of sick-related absence with greater regional fire activity. The intervention period was associated with approximately 29% lower indoor PM 2.5 after adjustment for outdoor PM 2.5 concentrations. Because this contrast pooled all randomized arms, including control, it should be interpreted as a period association rather than an independent HEPA or UVGI effect.

title: Investigation of individual and cohort-level temporal changes to legacy and emerging endocrine disrupting chemical exposures and their relationship with birth outcomes
abstract: Background Phthalates, parabens, and phenols co-occur in personal care and consumer products (PCPs). While policy and market-based campaigns have led to changes in product formulations, few studies have examined intra- and inter-individual changes in PCP chemical biomarkers in pregnant populations with birth outcomes. Objective Investigate changes in exposure to PCP-derived chemicals within and between pregnant women. Additionally, examine if exposures-individually and as a mixture-are associated with gestational age (GA) and birthweight z-scores (BWZ). Methods We collected maternal third-trimester urine samples from 299 Mothers and Newborns (MN, 2001-2006) and 246 Fair Start (FS, 2013-2021) New York City-based participants. A subset of MN (n = 62) provided urine at a subsequent pregnancy (Siblings cohort). We analyzed samples using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry for 16 phthalate, 4 paraben, and 5 environmental phenolic biomarkers. Paired t-tests and linear regression models compared intraindividual biomarker concentrations for participants that provided urine at two pregnancies. Linear regressions evaluated the interindividual differences in biomarker levels between cohorts. Linear regression and quantile g-computation were used to estimate the single- and multi-chemical relationships, respectively, with GA and BWZ for each cohort. Results Biomarkers of emerging contaminants di-(2-propylheptyl) phthalate and bisphenol S were higher in the FS cohort compared to the MN cohort in the interindividual analyses, and in subsequent pregnancies in the intraindividual analyses. Conversely, biomarkers of legacy chemicals (e.g., di-n-hexyl phthalate, di-(2-ethylhexyl phthalate)) were lower in the FS cohort and subsequent pregnancies compared to the MN cohort. Mono-hexyl phthalate was associated with earlier GA (β [95%CI]: -0.14 [-0.23, -0.05]) in the MN cohort. No significant mixture associations with GA and BWZ were observed. Significance Exposure to emerging contaminants has increased and exposure to legacy contaminants has decreased when assessing inter- and intra-individual urinary biomarker levels. Continued research is critical to better understand the health implications of emerging contaminants. Impact statement Higher levels of emerging chemicals (e.g., di-(2-propylheptyl) phthalate, bisphenol S) were found in a New York City-based cohort of women who provided urine samples between 2013 and 2021 compared to women who provided urine samples between 2001 and 2006. This demonstrates the need to include these contaminants in environmental epidemiologic studies to better understand their impacts on health. When exploring associations with birth outcomes, we identified a metabolite of di-n-hexyl phthalate, a legacy compound, to be associated with earlier gestational age only in the cohort from 2001 to 2006. This may indicate that temporal changes in exposure are important to health outcomes.
